etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Phonetic shift: /ariɡataku/ → /ariɡatau/ → /ariɡatoː/.
From ありがたく (arigataku), the adverbial form of Old Japanese and Classical Japanese adjective ありがたし (arigatashi, modern ありがたい arigatai, “grateful, thankful; welcome”), from 有り (ari, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, continuative or stem form) of verb 有る aru, “to exist, to be”) +‎ 難し (katashi, “hard, difficult”, 難い katai in modern Japanese). The katashi changes to gatashi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
Modern Japanese -i adjectives formerly ended in -ki for the attributive form. This medial /k/ dropped out during the Muromachi period, both for the attributive form (-ki becoming -i) and for the adverbial form (-ku becoming -u). However, the adverbial form reverted to -ku thereafter for most words, with the -u ending persisting in certain everyday set expressions, such as arigatō, おはよう (ohayō), or おめでとう (omedetō), and in hyper-formal speech.
Arigatashi is first attested in the oldest literature of the 8th century. It originally meant “difficult to exist, hard to be”, shifting to “rare, special”, and then to “welcome, thankful, nice to have” by some time in the 15th century. This sense is still in use:
この天(てん)気(き)はありがたいね。 ― Kono tenki wa arigatai ne. ― This weather sure is welcome (literally, “This weather sure is hard to come by”)
The similarity to Portuguese obrigado (“thank you”) is purely coincidental; the Portuguese first arrived in Japan in 1543, well over a century after citations expressing gratitude are found.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
As a surface analysis, this is a compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix) +‎ 母 (kā, “mother”) +‎ さん (-san, honorific suffix).
Historically, this represents a sound shift from older term o-kaka-sama, itself a compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix) +‎ 母 (kaka, “mother”) +‎ 様 (-sama, honorific suffix).
/okakasama/ → /okkasama/ → /okaːsama/
/okakasama/ → /okkasama/ → /okaːsan/
Attested in Osaka and Kyoto, with rare use in Edo (Tokyo), from the late Edo period, especially among upper-middle class households in Osaka.
Usage became widespread in the 20th century after the Ministry of Education adopted お父(とう)さん (otōsan, “father”) and お母(かあ)さん for use in 尋常小学読本 (Jinjō shōgaku dokuhon “Standard elementary school reader”, 1903).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix) +‎ 中 (naka, “insides; innards, stomach”). Originally coined as a deliberately indirect 女房詞 (nyōbō kotoba, “woman's word”) for 腹 (hara, “belly, gut”).
The use of the 腹 character to spell 中 (naka) appears to be a relatively recent shift; many dictionaries still list 御中 or お中 as the standard spelling for this term, but usage trends clearly show that this お腹 spelling is now more common for the belly senses.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First cited to 1924 in the novel Chijin no Ai (published in English as Naomi) by Jun’ichirō Tanizaki.
Although often described as wasei eigo (和製英語), this appears to derive from the English phrase salaried man, which appears in print at least as early as 1828. Additionally, the English noun phrase “salary man” also predates the Japanese term. The resulting Japanese term was reimported into English as a compound in the late 20th century.
The form is a regular phonological clipping of the borrowed phrase, dropping the English past‐participle suffix to fit Japanese phonotactics, analyzable as サラリー (sararī) +‎ マン (-man).
The term began to be used in the Taishō period and became firmly established by the early Shōwa period. Prior to its popularization, terms such as 月給取り, 俸給生活者, and 勤め人 were used for similar workers, alongside more derogatory terms like 腰弁当 and 洋服細民. Around 1960, the term ビジネスマン (bijinesuman) also started being used to avoid the mediocre image associated with this word.

Borrowed from French jupon (“petticoat, underskirt”), from French jupe (“skirt”), from old Italian jupa, from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba, “long garment”). Doublet of 襦袢.
Note that the meaning has changed from “underskirt” to “trousers/pants”, and the second consonant has changed from /p/ to /b/, possibly influenced by native Japanese onomatopoeia ずぼん (zubon), describing the action of something sliding into place, as when one puts on or takes off trousers.

etymologies.text:
/d͡ʑauzu/ → /d͡ʑɔːzu/ → /d͡ʑoːzu/
From Middle Chinese compound 上手 (dzyangH syuwX, “to have the upper hand → to gain mastery, to master something”, literally “top hand”).
This reading is likely a later innovation in Japanese after the initial borrowing. This uses the goon of jō for the first character, and the kan'yōon of zu for the second character.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/d͡ʑauɕu/ → /d͡ʑɔːɕu/ → /d͡ʑoːɕu/
From Middle Chinese compound 上手 (dzyangH syuwX, “to have the upper hand → to gain mastery, to master something”, literally “top hand”).
This is the goon reading for both characters, so likely the reading as initially borrowed.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/d͡ʑaute/ → /d͡ʑɔːte/ → /d͡ʑoːte/
Variation on jōzu above, replacing the kan'yōon of zu with the kun'yomi of te.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Compound of 上 (uwa, “up, upper”) +‎ 手 (te, “hand”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: Compound of 上 (kami, “up, upper”) +‎ 手 (te, “hand”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 6
etymologies.text:
/kamite/ → /kaũte/ → /kaute/ → /kɔːte/ → /koːte/
Shift from 上(かみ)手(て) (kamite).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 上(うわ) (uwa-, 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 上(うえ) (ue, “up; top”)) + 着(ぎ) (-gi, “clothes; -wear”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 着(き)る (kiru, “to wear”)). The ki changes to gi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Probably a semantic shift from 端 (heta, “edge of something”), referring metaphorically to the edge of one's abilities or knowledge.
The kanji spelling appears to be an instance of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Compound of 下 (shita, “down; under; lower”) +‎ 手 (te, “hand”).
Occasionally encountered with rendaku (連濁), where the -te ending changes to -de.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Compound of 下 (shimo, “lower”) +‎ 手 (te, “hand”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Compound of 下り (kudari, “descending”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 下る (kudaru, “to descend, to go down”)) +‎ 手 (te, “hand; side, direction”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 下手 (MC haeX|haeH syuwX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
A surface analysis suggests a Japanese coinage of Middle Chinese-derived components, as a compound of 下(げ) (ge, “lower, under”) + 駄(た) (ta, “loading, carrying; footwear”).
Historical usage suggests a shift from older term 足(あし)駄(だ) (ashida, “clogs”, later, referring more specifically to “tall clogs” in contrast to the “short clogs” referenced by the term 下(げ)駄(た) (geta)), itself deriving from 足(あし) (ashi, “foot”) + 板(いた) (ita, “board”), from the even older practice of wearing flat pieces of wood on one's feet when working in the paddies to keep from sinking into the mud, similar in principle to snowshoes. This latter footwear persisted in use into the 20th century as 田(た)下(げ)駄(た) (tageta, literally “paddy geta”).
The historical derivation indicates that the 駄 character's “footwear” sense, which is specific to Japanese and is not found in Chinese sources, could have arisen from phonetic ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)) usage in the terms 足(あし)駄(だ) (ashida) and 下(げ)駄(た) (geta).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 不足 (MC pjuw tsjowk, “not + enough”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 世界 (MC syejH keajH), originally a translation of Sanskrit लोकधातु (lokadhātu, “region or part of the world”). Compare Hokkien 世界 (sè-kài).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Two likely derivations:
From 二十(はた) (hata, “twenty”, by way of apophonic form hatsu-) + 日(か) (-ka, counter for days), or
A shift from 二十(はた)歳(ち) (hatachi, “twenty (years old)”) + 日(か) (-ka, counter for days):
/ɸatat͡ɕi ka/ → */ɸat̚t͡ɕɨka/ → /ɸat͡ɕuka/ → /hat͡ɕuka/
(Can this(+) etymology be sourced?)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From 二十 (nijū, “twenty”) +‎ 日 (nichi, “days”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese はたち (patati, “twenty items”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From 二十 (nijū, “twenty”) +‎ 歳 (sai, “year”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From 二十 (nijū, “twenty”) +‎ 歳 (sai, “year”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/putuka/ → /fut͡suka/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720.
Analyzable as a compound of 二 (futsu, “two”, irregular reading, apparently a shift from expected reading futa) +‎ 日 (ka, “day”, uncommon variant only occurring in certain compounds of ancient derivation).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Compound of 二 (futa, “two”, used in counting) +‎ 日 (hi, “day”). Generally only found in instances of counting, as in ひとひふたひ (hitohi futahi, “one day, two days...”).
First cited in 1746.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First attested in the Saibara.
Compound of 井 (i, “water well”) +‎ 所 (to, “place”). The to changes to do as an instance of rendaku (連濁)..

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 人形 (nyin heng, literally “person shape”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 人 (hito, “person”) +‎ 形 (kata, “shape, form”). The kata changes to gata as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 人(ひと) (hito, “person”) + 込(こ)み (komi, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 込(こ)む (komu, “to go into, be full of, have a lot of”).).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 人間 (MC nyin kean|keanH). Analyzable as a compound of "people" + "among; space".
First cited to a text from 984. The kanji spelling is cited earlier in a kanbun passage in the Shoku Nihongi of 756, listed in some references with the reading jinkan. However, the extant copies of this work that include phonetic guides are centuries younger than this first date, raising the possibility that the ningen reading might itself date from 756.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 人間 (MC nyin kean|keanH). Analyzable as a compound of "people" + "among; space".
First cited in a kanbun passage in the Shoku Nihongi of 756, listed in some references with the reading jinkan. However, the extant copies of this work that include phonetic guides are centuries younger than this first date, raising the possibility that the jinkan reading might be younger than this date.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: A compound of 人 (hito, “people”) +‎ 間 (ma, “gap”). First cited to the Nihon Shoki of 720, and also attested in the Man'yōshū of 759.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Compound of 此(こ) (ko, “this”) + 年(とし) (toshi, “year”).
The use of the kanji 今 (“now”) instead of 此 (“this”) is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 今年 (jīnnián).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 今年 (MC kim nen).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/kʲəm bʉan/ → /kombaɴ/
From Middle Chinese compound 今晚 (MC kim mjonX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Originally a compound of 此 (ke, “this”) +‎ 朝 (asa, “morning”).
The initial /ke/ is an alternative form of the initial /ko/ (此, “this”) seen in words such as ここ (koko, “this place → here”) or これ (kore, “this [nominal] → this”), and the final /sa/ is a contraction from */ke.asa/ to /kesa/ with the medial -a- falling out, as Old Japanese did not permit vowel clusters.
It is the same element found in 今日 (kepu→kyō, “today”).
The use of the kanji 今 (“now”) instead of 此 (“this”) is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/konteu/ → /kontjoː/
From Middle Chinese compound 今朝 (MC kim trjew, literally “now morning”). The /eu/ → /joː/ sound shift is a regular phonological change.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of し (shi, “doing”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb する suru “to do”) +‎ 上がる (agaru, “to go up, to be raised; to come to an end”). Compare the English expression to be done up → to be done thoroughly.
The 仕 kanji for the first character is an example of phonetic ateji.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From し (shi, “doing”, continuative form of する (suru, “to do”)) +‎ 事 (koto, “thing; stuff”). The koto reading for 事 changes to goto as an instance of rendaku (連濁). 仕 is ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From し (shi, “to do”, continuative form of する) + 方(かた) (kata, “method”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Compound of 仮(かり) (kari, “borrowing, provisional thing”, cognate with verb 借(か)る (karu, “to borrow”), the Old Japanese form of modern 借(か)りる (kariru)) + 名(な) (na, “name, character”), from the way that Chinese characters were borrowed for their phonetic values to spell out the sounds of native Japanese words.
Used in contrast to 真(ま)名(な) (mana, “true name, true character”), a synonym for 漢(かん)字(じ) (kanji), indicating Chinese characters used for their meaning instead of for their sound.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/karina/ → /kanna/
Contraction of 仮(かり)名(な) (karina) above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/karina/ → /kanna/ → /kana/
Contraction of 仮(かん)名(な) (kanna) above. The reading may appear to be jūbakoyomi, but is instead actually an irregular development of the kun'yomi.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 假名 (MC kaeX mjieng, literally “borrowed, false” + “name”). The kan'on reading, so probably a somewhat later borrowing from Chinese. Compare modern Cantonese reading gaa2 meng4-2.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text:
/kemjau/ → /kemjɔː/ → /kemjoː/
From Middle Chinese 假名 (MC kaeX mjieng, literally “borrowed, false” + “name”). The goon reading, so probably an earlier borrowing from Chinese. Compare modern Min Nan reading ké-miâ.
The Buddhist sense derives from use of this term in Chinese as a translation of Sanskrit प्रज्ञप्ति (prajñapti, “appointing → provisional naming”), used in some Buddhist schools to refer to the practice of conceptualising and naming things that are not real.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 仮名(かな) (kana, “kana”) + 遣(つか)い (tsukai, “use”).
The tsukai changes to zukai as an instance of rendaku (連濁)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From 小 (o, “little”) +‎ 母 (ha, “mother”). The kanji is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)). Compare 小母 (oba).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Chinese 伯母 (bómǔ, “paternal aunt”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese ただし, from ただ (tada, “just, but”) +‎ し (shi, emphatic particle).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Apparently coined in Japanese from Middle Chinese-derived elements, as a compound of 体 (tai, “body”) +‎ 操 (sō, “control, manipulate”). First cited in education-related materials from the early Meiji Period in the early 1870s, as part of educational reforms that included the addition of physical education to school curricula.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Appears to be a coinage in Japanese from Middle Chinese-derived roots, as a compound of 便 (ben, “convenience, ease”, also meaning “bodily waste; bowel movement”) +‎ 所 (sho, “place”). The sho changes to jo as an instance of rendaku (連濁). Compare English expressions seat of ease, house of ease, also pooper, shitter.
First cited in works from the late 1400s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
傘 (kasa): an umbrella.
 傘 on Japanese Wikipedia
From Old Japanese. Attested in a gloss of the Nihon Shoki (720) and Man'yōshū (759) in the ideographic spelling 笠. In turn, from reconstructed Proto-Japonic *kasa (“rain hat”). Possibly related to 重なる (kasanaru, “to overlap, to be layered”, intransitive), 重ねる (kasaneru, “to overlap, to layer”, transitive),.
The term originally refers to a bundle of reeds or sedges used as a rain hat. Following the spread of folding umbrellas in the 900s after their introduction from Baekje or China, the sense gradually shifted to also mean "umbrella".

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
傘 (karakasa): a traditional Japanese folding umbrella.
Compound of 唐 (kara, “Chinese; foreign”) +‎ 傘 (kasa, “raingear”). First attested in the Utsubo Monogatari of the late 900s.
Folding umbrellas were originally introduced from overseas, likely either Baekje or China, and this term was coined to refer specifically to this style of raingear, as distinct from the traditional Japanese rain hat.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 傘 (MC sanX). Not found in isolation.
The eighty sense is from 仐, the ryakuji or "abbreviated character" form of this kanji, which looks like 八 (“eight”) on top of 十 (“ten”), equating to 八十 (hachijū, “eighty”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 元氣 (MC ngjwon khj+jH, literally “first, fundamental, source + vapor, spirit, energy”). In Chinese cosmology, this represented the fundamental force that permeates all matter and life. Early Japanese borrowed this word and meaning. Later, this spelling was conflated with the meaning of homophone 減気 (genki, “recovery from illness”), adding in the modern senses related to healthy and wellness.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 元(もと) (moto, “origin, beginning”) + 気(き) (ki, “sense; mood; energy; spirit”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese of unclear derivation:
Probably originally a compound of 吾 (a, Eastern Old Japanese first-person pronoun) +‎ の (no, possessive particle) +‎ 兄 (ye → e, “eldest sibling”, see below):
⟨a no2 ye⟩ → */anʉʲɨe/ → /ani/
Alternatively, an apophonic form of 姉 (ane, “elder sister”), itself possibly from the same derivation above.
Several other theories have also been suggested.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
*/kwæi/ → /kʷæi/ → /keː/
From Middle Chinese 兄 (MC xjwaeng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/je/ → /e/
From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
Originally a compound of 子 (ko, “child”) +‎ の (no, possessive particle) +‎ 上 (kami, “upper”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
兄弟 on Japanese Wikipedia
From 兄 (kyō, “elder brother”, goon) +‎ 弟 (dai, “younger brother”, goon), from Middle Chinese 兄弟.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From 兄 (kei, “elder brother”, kan'on) +‎ 弟 (tei, “younger brother”, kan'on), from Chinese 兄弟. Compare 兄妹 (keimai, “elder brother and younger sister”), 姉弟 (shitei, “elder sister and younger brother”), and 姉妹 (shimai, “elder and younger sisters”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 先生 (MC sen sraeng, literally “born earlier”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Compound of 先 (saki, “point, tip; the front, the forward direction; the future”) +‎ 行き (yuki, “going”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 行く (yuku, “to go”), alternative reading for iku).
The sakiyuki reading is first cited to a text from 1678.
Less commonly encountered with the reading sakiiki, using the standard iki reading for the second half. This variant is first cited to a text from 1686.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Ultimately from Middle Chinese 先行 (MC sen haeng, literally “preceding + to go”).
First cited to a text from 833.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 先輩 (MC sen pwojH). Doublet of ソンベ (sonbe).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Classical Japanese 八日(やうか) (yauka), itself usually considered a shift from 八日(やか) (yaka), ultimately a compound of 八(や) (ya, “eight”) + 日(か) (-ka, counter for days). There is speculation that -uka was the original counter for days (see the etymology at 日(か) (ka)), in which case yauka may have been the older form and yaka a shift from that.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 八(や) (ya, “eight”) + 日(か) (-ka, counter for days). Possibly instead a shift from 八日(やうか) (yauka).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 二 (futa, “two”) +‎ 度 (-tabi, counter for times).
The okurigana び (​bi) is used to indicate the reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Analyzed by references as either a compound of 再来 (sarai, “two next, the one after next”) +‎ 月 (getsu, “month”), or as a compound of 再 (sa, “again, one more”) +‎ 来月 (raigetsu, “next month”).
First attested in 1799.

etymologies.text: Compound of 爪 (tsume, “claw”) +‎ 痛い (itai, “painful”), with the medial /-i-/ falling out.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Shift from tsumetai above.
First attested in at least 1889.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/herikomu/ → /hekomu/
Contraction of 減りこむ (herikomu), itself a compound of 減り (heri, “lessening, becoming less”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 減る heru, “to reduce, to become less”) +‎ 込む (komu, “to go inwardly”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: (This term, 凹む, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
出(で)る (deru, “to exit”) + 口(くち) (kuchi, “opening, door”).
The kuchi changes to guchi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From 切(きっ)符(ぷ) (kippu, “a ticket used for public transport”) + 手(て)形(がた) (tegata, “commercial paper”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: (This term, 切手, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 刺(さ)し (sashi, “sticking into, sticking between; slicing”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 刺(さ)す (sasu, “to stick into”)) + 身(み) (mi, “flesh, meat”). The use of the verb 刺(さ)す (sasu) here to mean slice is irregular, and may be due to the kill connotations of the verb 切(き)る (kiru, “to cut, to slice”) during the Muromachi period when the word sashimi first appears.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 髪 (kami, “hair on the head”) +‎ 剃り (sori, “shaving facial hair or body hair; a shaver”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 剃(そ)る (soru, “to shave facial hair or body hair”).). First cited in the ten-volume Wamyō Ruijushō of 934 CE.
The kanji are from Chinese 剃刀 (tìdāo).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 努力 (MC nuX lik, literally “to exert + strength”). Compare modern Cantonese reading nou5 lik6 or Min Nan ló͘-le̍k.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Attested in the Kojiki of 712. From Proto-Japonic *unkoku.
Likely derived as a compound of うご (ugo, a 擬態語 (gitaigo, “mimetic word”) imitative of something crawling or creeping; compare the sound shapes of roots wrig- or wig- in English wriggle, wiggle) +‎ く (ku, verb-forming suffix). Compare also the related adverb うごうご (ugougo, “wrigglingly, squirmingly, creepingly: moving in continuous small increments”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Rare dialectal variation on ugoku above.
Attested from the late Muromachi period (1336–1573).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
Rare dialectal variation on ugoku above.
Attested in a text from 1002.

From 玉 (tama, “ball”) +‎ 子 (ko, “child, small thing”). The ko reading for 子 changes to go as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Appears to be a learned borrowing from Chinese 友好 (yǒuhǎo). First attested in 1900.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 友(とも) (tomo, “friend”) + 好(よし) (yoshi, “good”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 友(とも) (tomo, “friend”) + 達(たち) (-tachi, pluralizing suffix). Originally plural, but also used in the singular sense in modern Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
双(ふた) (futa, “set of two”) + 子(こ) (ko, “child”)
The ko changes to go as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 召し (meshi, “taking”, stem of Old Japanese honorific verb mesu, “to see, to look at”, by extension an honorific for “to take, to eat”) +‎ 上がる (agaru, “to rise”, used honorifically to mean “to take up, to eat”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:可愛い
Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Kawaii
Wikipedia
/kawajui/ → /kawaiː/
Shift in pronunciation from kawayui below.
The kanji spelling 可愛い is an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)), and uses an irregular reading of 愛. The phonological resemblance to Mandarin 可愛 (kě'ài), Min Nan 可愛 (khó-ài, “lovable”) is coincidental. Note that the medial -w- here is not an excrescence added between ka (可) and ai (愛), since the word is not formed from these morphemes.
Already realized phonetically as /kawaiː/ by the early 1600s, and possibly found alongside older form kawayui, as seen in the 1603 edition of the Nippo Jisho.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From classical Japanese /kawo hajuɕi/ → /kawajui/.
A contraction of classical 顔映し (kawahayushi, “embarrassing, shameful”). The meaning underwent an ameliorative semantic shift from shameful to evoking pity, to evoking compassion, and then to lovable. The kanji spelling appears to be jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), from the above reading. Compare Korean 예쁘다 (yeppeu-da), which originally meant poor (as in "poor, poor kid") but now means pretty.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 可能 (khaX nong, literally “may, can + able, ability”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Probably originally a compound of 競り (seri, “hawking, calling out in a loud voice”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 競る (seru), “to hawk, to call out in a loud voice”) +‎ 言ふ (ifu, ancient spelling of modern 言う (iu), “to say”):
*/seri ipu/ → */seripu/ → /seriɸu/ → /serifu/
Alternatively, the final -fu may have come instead from 合ふ (afu), ancient form of modern 合う (au, “to do something together”) (thus, a doublet of 競り合う):
*/seri apu/ → */seripu/ → /seriɸu/ → /serifu/
The kanji spelling is from the synonymous Middle Chinese-derived daishi reading below.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 臺詞 (MC doj zi). Uses the goon reading for the first character and the kan'on reading for the second character, suggesting either a pronunciation shift within Japanese, or influence from a Chinese dialect or later pronunciation.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First attested in Japanese in 1900 in the katakana form タイフーン (taifūn), itself a borrowing from English typhoon.
Prior to the Meiji era (1868–1912), this kind of severe storm was called a 野分き (nowaki), literally a "field-splitter" for the way the winds would wreak havoc on farms. The term タイフーン (taifūn) then appears in 1900, also attested with spelling 大風 and reading of taifun. Then in 1907 meteorologist Okada Takematsu (岡田武松) scientifically defined what qualifies as this specific type of storm, and then purportedly as phono-semantic matching of the English typhoon, adopted the kyūjitai kanji spelling 颱風 (read as taifū without that final "n") on the basis of Chinese references using the term 颱風 / 台风 (táifēng). This spelling then became common from the Taisho era (1912–1926).
There was likely some influence from Chinese on the form of the Japanese word. In Walter Henry Medhurst's English and Chinese Dictionary of 1847-48, he glossed the English word typhoon as Chinese 太風 / 太风 and 颶風 / 飓风 (jùfēng), the former of which would be read in Japanese as taifū.
The origins of English typhoon are somewhat uncertain, with possible ancient connections to Chinese. See that entry for more.
台 is a daiyōji replacing 颱.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Derived from 名 (na, “name”) +‎ 前 (mae, front). Compare the semantics of Latin praenomen.
Appears as a term only in the last few centuries, becoming more widely used during the Meiji period.
Similarity to English name and other Indo-European words derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ is coincidental.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 吹雪く (fubuku, “to blow violently (said of wind); to blow a snowstorm”).
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), borrowed from Chinese 吹雪 (chuīxuě).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
⟨mi1so1⟩ → /miso/
From Old Japanese. First attested in Ritsuryō tax records from 738 CE, with the spelling 未醤.
Possibly also attested with the spelling 末醤 on a mokkan (wooden tally stick) dated to the reign of Emperor Junnin during the years 758–764, although this might be a different word, as 未 and 末 are distinct characters with separate pronunciations and opposite meanings.
Phonetically recorded as 美蘇 in the Wamyō Ruijushō of 938, but the commentary describes this as erroneously written as 未醤.
Vovin considers it to be a borrowing from Koreanic, compare Modern Korean 메주 (meju) "brick of dried fermented soybeans." This is supported by the Ruijushō citing the Youshikangosho saying that it is a "Korean sauce".
Cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *miso. A Proto-Japonic *misV is sometimes reconstructed as the ancestor for both if Ryukyuan didn't borrow it directly from Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb せく (seku, “to cough”). Cognate with 堰 (seki, “dam”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
By surface analysis, 哲(てつ) (tetsu, “clear, wise, sage”) + 学(がく) (-gaku, “study”). Coined by Nishi Amane in his 1874 百一新論 as a translation of English philosophy or Dutch filosofie. Nishi's kanji spelling 希哲學 (hirosohi) is literally calqued from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía, “pursuit of wisdom”, literally “love of knowledge”), apparently from the Chinese morphemes 希 (xī, “to long for”) and 哲 (zhé, “wisdom”), before he later settled with 哲學 (modernly spelt 哲学).
Nishi also used the transcriptions ヒロソヒ, ヒロソヒー (hirosohī) and 斐鹵蘇比.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 商人 (MC syang nyin).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Shift from あきびと (akibito).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Shift from あきびと (akibito).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
Superficially あき (aki, “trade”) +‎ ひと (hito, “person”). Possibly Old Japanese.
Aki can also be found as the root of あきなう (akinau, “to trade”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, in turn from Middle Chinese 器械 (MC khijH heajH, “apparatus; weapon”, literally “utensil; tool + weapon; implement”).
First appears in Japanese in a text from 718 CE with the 器械 spelling and a sense of weapon.
Later appears in a text from 1520 as 機械 (kikai) with a sense of apparatus, device, machine, mechanism, replacing 器 (ki, “utensil; tool”) with 機 (ki, “weaving loom; apparatus”) and reflecting changes in usage and meaning. This spelling may be a Japanese innovation, and it only becomes prominent from around 1874. Prior to that, this term was more commonly written with the original 器械 spelling.
In modern Japanese, some definitions distinguish the 機械 and 器械 spellings with 機械 used for those machines that include their own motive power, and 器械 for those that have no power of their own. General usage appears to be broader, differentiating the two spellings by the size of the item, with 器械 used for a smaller apparatus or device, and 機械 used for a larger apparatus or equipment. These broad distinctions generally also hold true for the suffixes 器 (-ki) and 機 (-ki).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 國境 (MC kwok kjaengX). First attested in a portion of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 706.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Compound of 国(くに) (kuni, “province; country”) + 境(さかい) (sakai, “border”). The sakai changes to zakai as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First attested in 1660.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 國民 (MC kwok mjin).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of native Japanese words: 国 (kuni, “country”) +‎ 民 (tami, “people”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 国 (koku, “nation”) +‎ 語 (go, “language”). The sense of "Mandarin" is derived from Taiwanese usage of the identical Chinese word 國語／国语 (guóyǔ).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/doeubi/ > /dojoːbi/
Compound of 土曜 (doyō, “Saturn (the planet)”, in reference also to the day for that planet, as originally imported from Chinese astrology in the Heian period) +‎ 日 (hi, “day”). The hi changes to bi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
The compound form suffixed with 日 (hi, “day”) appears in common use from the Meiji period with the promulgation of the Gregorian calendar. See also Names of the days of the week on Wikipedia.Wikipedia

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Probably a compound of 宮 (miya, “shrine”) +‎ 笥 (ke, “small box”).
The ke changes to ge as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Superficially of 土(ど) (do, “land, ground”) + 産(さん) (san, “production, produce”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/di t͡ɕin/ → /d͡ʑiɕiɴ/
From Old Japanese, in turn from Middle Chinese compound 地震 (MC dijH tsyinH). First cited to a text from 734.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/nawi/ → */nawʲi/ → /naji/ → /nai/
From Old Japanese. First cited to 720 in the Nihon Shoki.
Apparently this term semantically first referred to the ground, and was used most in constructions like ないふる (naifuru, “the ground shakes”). Over time, this shifted via metonymy to refer to the shaking itself.
May be a compound of 土(な) (na, “ground”, possibly an apophonic form of ni, "earth, soil") + 居(ゐ) (i, “being”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of 居(ゐ)る (iru, “to be”, in a location; in modern Japanese, used of animate objects)).
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/nawi/ → */nawʲi/ → /naji/ → /naje/ → /nae/
Appears in the Nippo Jisho.
Shift from nai, historical nawi (see above). First cited to the late 1400s.
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: Compound of 地 (ji, “ground”) +‎ 震い (furui, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of classical Japanese verb 震ふ (furufu, “to tremble; to roar”), related to modern 震える (furueru)). The furui changes to burui as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 基(もと) (moto, “base, foundation”) + 付(つ)く (tsuku). The tsuku changes to zuku as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
塩 (shio): a close-up picture of salt crystals.
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:塩
Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Salt
Wikipedia
⟨sipo⟩ → /ɕiɸo/ → /ɕiwo/ → /ɕio/
From Old Japanese, cited in the Kojiki of 712 CE. The Old Japanese term is cognate to Ainu シㇷ゚ポ (sippo) and Ainu シㇱポ (sispo).
Cognate with 潮 (shio, “[ocean] tide”).
The medial consonant had already lenited to /w/ by 1603, as recorded in the Nippo Jisho.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 鹽 (MC yem, “salt”) and 鹽 (MC yemH, “to salt; salting”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 処(か) (ka, “place”) + 重(へ) (he, “division”), in reference to walls dividing objects apart. The he changes to be as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compound of 夜(よ) (yo, “night”) + 中(なか) (naka, “middle”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Apparently from Middle Chinese 夜中 (MC yaeH trjuwng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Compound of 夜(よ) (yo, “night”) + 中(ちゅう) (-chū, “during, throughout”, rendaku form 中(じゅう) (jū)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text:
⟨i me2⟩ → */jiməɨ/ → /jɨme/ → /jume/
Shift from Old Japanese 夢 (ime2), itself a compound of 寝 (i, “sleep, sleeping”, obsolete) +‎ 目 (me, “eye; sight, vision”).
Appears in texts from the 900s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 夢 (MC mjuwngH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 大 (tai, “big”) +‎ した (shita, “did, done”), the perfective of する (suru, “to do”), used here to indicate a state as opposed to an action.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 大人(おとな) (otona, “adult”) + しい (-shii, adjectivizing suffix).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Likely a shift in reading of taizei below, adopting the native-Japanese kun'yomi of ō for the first character.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Shift in reading of taisei below. Ultimately from Middle Chinese 大勢 (MC dajH syejH). Uses the kan'yōon of zei for the second character, indicating a shift in pronunciation after borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 大勢 (MC dajH syejH). The kan'on, so likely the reading as borrowed from Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
大(おお) (ō-, “large”) + 通(とお)り (tōri, “street”).
The tōri changes to dōri as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:天皇
Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Emperor of Japan
Wikipedia
From Middle Chinese 天皇 (MC then hwang) with the original sense of “heavenly sovereign”.
The 呉(ご)音(おん) (goon, literally “Wu sound”) pronunciation, so likely the initial borrowing from Middle Chinese. The ō reading for 皇 changes to nō as an instance of renjō (連(れん)声(じょう)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:天皇 (三皇)
Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Heavenly Sovereign
Wikipedia
/ten kʷau/ → /tenkʷɔː/ → /tenkɔː/ → /tenkoː/
From Middle Chinese 天皇 (MC then hwang).
The 漢(かん)音(おん) (kan'on, literally “Han sound”) pronunciation, so likely a later borrowing from Middle Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/sumeraɡi/ → /suberaɡi/
Shift from sumeragi below, with the nasal /m/ becoming a plosive /b/.
The kanji spelling is from tennō above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
⟨sume1ro2ki1⟩ → */sumʲerəkʲi/ → */sumeraki/ → /sumeraɡi/
Possibly a shift from Old Japanese 天皇 (sume1ro2ki1).
The kanji spelling is from tennō above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text:
From 皇(すめら) (sumera-, prefix of praise and respect) + 君(きみ) (kimi, “lord, master → sovereign”). The kimi changes to gimi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
The kanji spelling is from tennō above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 6
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese.
From 皇(すめら) (sumera-, prefix of praise and respect) + 尊(みこと) (mikoto, “Highness”).
The kanji spelling is from tennō above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compound of 女 (onna, “a woman; female”) +‎ の (no, appositional particle) +‎ 子 (ko, “a child”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Compound of 女 (me, “a woman; female”) +‎ の (no, appositional particle) +‎ 子 (ko, “a child”).
Less commonly used than onnanoko above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Probably ultimately from Middle Chinese 女房 (MC nrjoX bjang), with an initial meaning in line with the spelling: 女 (woman) + 房 (“room, chamber”). First cited to 985.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/njoːboː/ → /njoːbo/
Shortening of the final vowel in 女房 (nyōbō).
First cited to 1752.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
Shift from 女房 (nyōbō).
First cited to a text from the late 1100s.
This form of the word gained greater currency during the Muromachi period (1336–1573), then fell out of use in the early Edo period (1603–1868). It is possible that this form of the word is simply an orthographical variant; various Japanese references indicate that it might have still been pronounced as something like nyōbō.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
⟨imo1⟩ → */imʷo/ → /imo/
From Old Japanese 妹 (imo1). First cited in the Kojiki of 712.
Speculatively, may be related to terms such as 女 (me1, womi1na, “woman”), 嫗 (omi1na, “elderly woman”), and 母 (omo, “mother”), wherein the medial /-m-/ appears to signify woman, female. However, the difference in vowel values presents a difficulty.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/imo ɸito/ → /imowito/ → */imowuto/ → /imoːto/
Originally a compound of 妹 (imo, “sister, close female companion”) +‎ 人 (hito, “person”). First cited in The Tales of Ise of the early 900s.
This is an instance of ウ音便 (u onbin, “u sound shift”), found in terms with bilabial consonants (/m/, /b/, /w/) followed by i; commonly seen in terms such as 玄人 (kurōto, “professional”), 素人 (shirōto, “amateur”), or possibly, 相撲 (sumō, “sumo”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
Analyzed as a shortening of imōto, itself a compound 妹 (imo, “sister, close female companion”) +‎ 人 (hito, “person”).
Appears in The Tale of Heiji, written around the mid-12th century. May be much older, as this reading is also included in kun'yomi glosses for the Nihon Shoki of 720 (although the manuscripts with the glosses themselves are not as old).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 妹 (MC mwojH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese of unclear derivation:
Probably originally a compound of 吾 (a, Eastern Old Japanese first-person pronoun) +‎ の (no, possessive particle) +‎ 兄 (ye → e, “eldest sibling”):
⟨a no2 ye⟩ → */anʉʲɨe/ → /ane/
An apophonic form of 兄 (ani, “elder brother”).
Several other theories have also been suggested.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 姓名 (MC sjengH mjieng, literally “surname, clan name + name, given name”). The reading is kan'on, so likely a later borrowing. Compare modern Min Nan reading sèⁿ-miâ.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/siaumiau/ → /ɕjɔːmjɔː/ → /ɕoːmjoː/
From Middle Chinese 姓名 (MC sjengH mjieng, literally “surname, clan name + name, given name”). The goon, so likely the initial borrowing. Compare modern Hakka reading siang-miàng.
Rare in modern Japanese. Largely superseded by the seimei reading above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Compound of 姓 (kabane, “clan”) +‎ 名 (na, “name”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compound of 目(ま) (ma-, “eye, sight”, archaic) + 守(も)る (moru, “protect, watch over”, Etymology 2). まぼる and まぶる are alterations of まもる.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Related to 目 (me, “eye”) and 見る (miru, “to see, to look at”), with an underlying meaning of to watch over.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 安心 (MC 'an sim). Compare modern Chinese 安心 (ānxīn).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Ultimately from Middle Chinese compound 安心 (MC 'an sim), likely through 安(あん)心(しん) (anshin) above. The shin changes to jin as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text:
⟨ipe1⟩ → /ipʲe/ → /iɸe/ → /iwe/ → /ie/
From Old Japanese. Possibly cognate with Old Korean 邑勒 (iprʌk, “house”).
Possibly related to 廬 (iho → io, “temporary hut”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text:
Inherited from Old Japanese [Term?], from Proto-Japonic *utui.
Doublet of 内(うち) (uchi, “middle, inside”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3 2
etymologies.text:
Contraction of uchi above.
Often following the genitive case marker の (no) which contracts to -n.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4 2
etymologies.text: (This term, 家, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 家 (MC kae).
The 漢音 (kan'on, literally “Han sound”), so likely a latter borrowing from Middle Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 6
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 家 (MC kae).
The 呉音 (goon, literally “Wu sound”), so likely the initial borrowing from Middle Chinese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Early Middle Japanese adjective 寒(さむ)し (samushi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i).
Starting in at least the Muromachi period, this term became sporadically pronounced with a medial /b/ as 寒(さぶ)し (sabushi) (not to be confused with 寂(さぶ)し (sabushi), original form of 寂(さび)しい (sabishii)). Compare the similar /m/~/b/ alternation seen in 寂しい (sabishii, samishii, “lonely, desolate”), 頭 (tsuburi, tsumuri, “head”), and 煙 (keburi, kemuri, “smoke”). Related to 冷(さ)む (samu, “to cool down”), modern 冷(さ)める (sameru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 寝 (ne, “sleeping”, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “the continuative or stem form”) of verb 寝る (neru, “to sleep”)) +‎ 坊 (bō, “boy”, term of endearment).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 小(こ) (ko, “little”) + 包(つつ)み (tsutsumi, “package”). The tsutsumi changes to zutsumi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From 小 (shō, “small”) +‎ 説 (setsu, “narrative, story”).
(This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium. Particularly: “coined by 坪内逍遥 acc. to daijisen”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:少女
Wikipedia ja
少女 (shōjo): a girl holding a puppy.
From Middle Chinese compound 少女 (MC syewX|syewH nrjoX|nrjoH). Compare modern Mandarin 少女 (shàonǚ).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Originally a compound of 乙 (oto, “young, little”) +‎ 女 (me, “female, girl”). Compare 男 (otoko, “man”), originally meaning "young boy".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/seunen/ → /ɕeunen/ → /ɕoːnen/
Borrowing from Middle Chinese 少年 (syewH nen, literally “young + years”). Compare modern Cantonese 少年 (siu3 nin4), Mandarin 少年 (shàonián), Korean 소년 (sonyeon), Vietnamese thiếu niên.
Originally referred to young people of either gender. The meaning has narrowed in modern usage to more commonly refer to boys of elementary school or middle school age.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:山
Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Mountain
Wikipedia
From Old Japanese 山 (yama). First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Reconstructed as deriving in turn from Proto-Japonic *yama (“mountain; forest”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 山 (MC srean).
Sometimes spelled with rendaku (連濁), as -zan.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, itself apparently a borrowing from Old Korean. See Korean 뫼 (moe) for more.
The phonetic man'yōgana spelling 牟礼 for mure appears first in the Kojiki of 720 CE, but instead for the stem of verb 群れる (mureru, “to group together”). The first instance of this spelling for the mountain sense is in the Heian period, in different 日本書紀私記 (Nihon Shoki Shiki) versions, themselves recompilations of the Nihon Shoki. This reading with this sense apparently arises from the traditional 訓読 (kundoku) of a particular section of the Nihon Shoki, where the written word 山 is read as mure with an apparent meaning of mountain or hill.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 川 (kapa), from Proto-Japonic *kapa.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from Literary Chinese, possibly early Mandarin 蒲團／蒲团 (pútuán), likely as part of the importation of Zen Buddhism, for which practice these were originally used. First cited in Japanese to a text from the early-mid 1200s with the "meditation cushion" sense.
Originally referred literally to a 蒲 (pú, “bulrush, cattail”) 團／团 (tuán, “ball”), from the way these were round cushions made from woven bulrush leaves.
After the term was borrowed, the usage and construction of these cushions changed and the connection with bulrushes was weakened, leading to the simpler character 布 (fu, “cloth”) being used as a replacement for 蒲 (fu, “bulrush, cattail”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of Old Japanese 常 (tsune, “constancy, permanence, forever”) +‎ に (ni, adverbial particle).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 平 (hira, “flat, smooth”) +‎ 仮名 (kana). The kana changes to gana as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compound of 平(ひら) (hira, “broad, flat”) + 日(ひ) (hi, “day”). The hi of 日 changes to bi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 平日 (MC bjaeng nyit).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Possibly from Old Japanese. Japanese dictionaries cite the word to the Nihon Shoki (720), but only where kana glosses read 不賢 (literally “not mature; not capable”) as ヲサナシ (wosanasi). The first actual phonetic attestation is in the Shinsen Jikyō (898-901), as 乎佐奈志.
Compound of 長 (osa, “chief, senior”) +‎ 無い (nai, “not”, from classical 無し (nashi)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 幼稚 (yōchi, “infantile”) +‎ 園 (en, “garden”). The term is apparently a calque of German Kindergarten (“children's garden”), as Japanese yōchien were started in 1876 based on the German model initiated by Friedrich Fröbel in 1837 and on the term Kindergarten that he coined in 1840.
First cited in Japanese to 1876.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Attested in the 日(に)本(ほん)書(しょ)紀(き) (Nihon Shoki), completed in 720 and one of the earliest works written in Japanese, with a meaning of “bed”.
According to the 和(わ)句(く)解(げ) (Wakuge), published in 1668 by early Edo-period scholar 松(まつ)永(なが)貞(てい)徳(とく) (Matsunaga Teitoku), derives from 行(ゆ)か (yuka), the 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) stem of the verb 行(ゆ)く (yuku, “to go”), of an original meaning similar to “not going”, in reference to a place where one sits down to rest.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
⟨to2ko2⟩ → /toko/
From Old Japanese. Cognate with 所 (tokoro, “place”). Attested since at least the Nara period, appearing in the Man'yōshū, completed in 759.
Possibly an ancient compound of ⟨to1⟩ (Proto-Japonic *to (“place”), as in 跡 ⟨ato1⟩, “footprint, track”, from “foot place, where one has stepped”) + ⟨ko2⟩ (noun-forming suffixing element denoting “place”, as in ここ ⟨ko2ko2⟩, “here”, from “this place”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/ʑau/ → /ɕau/ → /ɕɔː/ → /ɕoː/
From Middle Chinese 床 (MC dzrjang). Devoicing apparently occurred after borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Short for earlier 見(み)せ棚(だな) (misedana), from 見(み)せる (miseru, “to show”) + 棚(たな) (tana, “shelf”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 店 (MC temH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compound of 座(ざ) (za, “seat”) + 布団(ふとん) (futon, “futon”). The futon reading for 布団 changes to buton as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
A compound of 座 (za, “sitting”) +‎ 敷 (shiki, “spreading, covering”), the stem noun form of verb 敷く (shiku, “to spread or lay out on the floor or ground”).
Japanese houses originally had wood floors, and mats or cushions called 座 (za) would be laid out (敷く (shiku)) for sitting upon. Tatami (畳) flooring did not become common until some time during the Muromachi Period, approximately 1337 to 1573.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/bentau/ → /bentɔː/ → /bentoː/.
Probably a variant of 面(めん)筒(とう) (mentō, “(obsolete) tub for distributing portions of food”), from 面(めん) (men, “face”) + 筒(とう) (tō, “bucket, tub”) (originally referring to a tub for washing the face), both from Middle Chinese.
The use of 弁 for ben is an example of phonetic ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)), due to 便 having another sense of “human excrement”.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Shift from 弁(べん)当(とう) (bentō) above, shortening the vowel.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 弟子 (MC dejX tsiX). Probably the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Appears to be a shift from teishi above. This is now the most common reading for the disciple, apprentice sense.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: (This term, 弟子, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: First appears in writing in the late Edo period as a compound of 彼の (kano, ano, “that”) +‎ 女 (onna, “woman”) with the reading kano onna or ano onna, simply meaning “that woman”. The kanojo reading arose by replacing the kun'yomi reading of onna for the second character with its on'yomi of jo. The first written appearance of the kanojo reading is in 1876, in the 改正画引小学読本 (Kaisei Gakubiki Shōgaku Dokuhon, “Revised Stroke-ordered Elementary-school Reader”). The first clear use of this term as a pronoun is around 1888, arising out of influence from Western works. The kanojo reading became more common and replaced kano onna and ano onna during the Taishō period (1912-1926).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix) +‎ 中 (naka, “inside; middle”). Originally coined as a 女房詞 (nyōbō kotoba, “woman's word”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 御 (on-, honorific prefix) +‎ 中 (chū, “inside; middle”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Compound of 御 (o-, honorific prefix) +‎ 中 (chū, “inside; middle”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compound of 御 (go-, honorific prefix) +‎ 飯 (han, “cooked rice”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 頬 (hoho, “cheek”) +‎ 笑む (emu, “smile”).
The spelling appears to be an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), based on Chinese 微笑 (wēixiào, literally “slight smile”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 思(おも)い (omoi, “thought”) + 出(で) (de, “something coming out”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 思(おも)い (omoi, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 思(おも)う (omou, “to think”)) + 出(だ)す (dasu, “to take out”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 恋(こい) (koi, “love”) + 人(ひと) (-hito, “person”). The hito changes to bito as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Sources are agreed that modern osoraku as an adverb is a clipping of older noun phrase 恐らくは (osoraku wa), trimming off the topic particle は (wa). This clipped form first appears in the late 1500s. Speculatively, this usage might have been influenced by the -ku adverbial ending used for adjectives.
Past there, different sources give different derivations for the osoraku portion itself.
May be from the -ku nominalization of verb 恐る (osoru, “to fear, to be afraid of”), originally a 四段活用 (yodan katsuyō, “quadrigrade-conjugation”) verb. In the traditional analysis, the く (ku) noun-forming suffix attaches to the 未然形 (mizenkei, “irrealis form”) of the verb stem, ending in -a: osoru (plain form) → osora- (irrealis) + -ku (noun-forming suffix) = osoraku.
Older documents also record a form 恐るらくは (osoruraku wa), which may be from 恐る (osoru, “to fear, to be afraid of”) as either a 上二段活用 (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade-conjugation”) or 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade-conjugation”) verb. In the traditional analysis, for bigrade verbs, the く (ku) noun-forming suffix manifests instead as らく (raku) and attaches to the 終止形 (shūshikei, “terminal or predicative form”) of the verb, the standard "plain" or "dictionary form" ending in -u: osoru + -raku = osoruraku.
The irregularities in the verb form required for -ku nominalization, and the shifts between bare -ku and longer form -raku, can be resolved if the underlying form of the nominalizing suffix were -aku instead, syntactically acting as a noun, and thus requiring that the verb be in the 連体形 (rentaikei, “adnominal form”). Also, Old Japanese did not allow hiatus (consecutive vowels without an intervening consonant), forcing either vowel fusion or vowel elision. For bigrade osoru, we would have adnominal form osoruru + suffix -aku, with the final -u in osoruru eliding to give us attested osoruraku.
*/osoruru aku wa/ → /osoruraku wa/ → /osoraku wa/ → /osoraku/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 生(む)す (musu, “to beget”) + 子(こ) (ko, “child”). 息 is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), from Middle Chinese 息子.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from 感ずる (kanzuru), a compound of 感 (kan, “feeling”) +‎ する (suru, “to do, to be”). Natural progression from サ行変格活用 (sa-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “s-irregular conjugation”) verbs ending in -uru to 上一段活用 (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Originally derived from verb 懐(なつ)く (natsuku, “to get used to and keep close; to become fond of”), itself an abbreviation of 馴(な)れ付(つ)く (naretsuku) of the same meaning. The adjective originally described wanting to keep something close, wanting to express fondness for something. Over time, this term was used more to describe reminiscences, leading to the modern meaning.
First attested in the Man'yōshū poetry anthology completed in 759 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 手 (te, “hand”) +‎ 伝う (tsutau, “to go along something (intransitive); to move something along, to transmit something (transitive)”).
The expected form of such a compound would be either てつたう (tetsutau), or てづたう (tezutau) with rendaku. The actual attested form of てつだう (tetsudau) suggests metathesis, with the voicing of rendaku shifting from the tsu to the following ta.
First attested in the late 1500s in 狂言 (kyōgen, “popular plays”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compound of Old Japanese elements 手 (te, “hand”) +‎ 前 (mae, “front”), originally meaning “that which is just in front of one's hand”.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Corruption of temae. The vowel shift emphasizes the confrontational sense of the term. This flattening of diphthongs to monophthongs is characteristic of Tokyo's Shitamachi dialect. Compare おめえ (omē, from お前 (omae)), ねえ (nē, from ない), やべえ (yabē, from やばい (yabai)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 手 (te, “hand”) +‎ 帳 (chō, “notebook, ledger”). Appears from the early 1600s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Compound of 手 (te, “hand”) +‎ 紙 (kami, “paper”). The kami changes to gami as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
An etymologically unrelated false friend of Chinese 手紙 / 手纸 (shǒuzhǐ).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/teɡami/ → /teɡaɴ/
Shift from standard Japanese tegami, dropping the final vowel and keeping the nasal.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 手(て) (te, “hand”) + 袋(ふくろ) (fukuro, “bag”). The fukuro reading for 袋 changes to bukuro as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 受ける (ukeru, “to receive”) +‎ 賜る (tamawaru, “to be granted”), with alternative (irregular) spelling as 受け賜る.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From 振(ふ)り (furi, “assigning”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 振(ふ)る (furu, “to assign, to stick on, to apportion”)) + 仮名(かな) (kana, “kana”).
The kana changes to gana as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
First attested in 1813.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally a compound of 言 (koto, “words”) +‎ 割る (waru, “split”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/arataɕi/ → /ataraɕi/ → /ataraɕiki/ → /ataraɕiː/
In Old Japanese, the original term was 新たし (aratashi), composed of older 新た (arata, “new”) + adjective-forming suffix し (shi). This persisted until at least the mid-1200s, and indeed the adjective stem arata is both modern adjective 新た (arata, -na adjective) and the root of verbs such as 改める (aratameru, “to renew, refresh, revise, or reform something”). See 新た (arata) for further details of that etymology.
Starting from the 900s, the aratashi reading began shifting to atarashi. This metathesis may have been due to conflation with 可惜し (atarashi, “magnificent, excellent, precious; regrettable”). The aratashi reading then became more and more uncommon in Early Middle Japanese, and the “new, modern, fresh” sense became the main use, superseding the largely homophonous 可惜し (atarashi) and pushing it out of common usage.
The modern form is from Early Middle Japanese adjective 新(あたら)し (atarashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in しき (shiki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of しい (shii).
Displaced Old Japanese 新し (nipisi, adjective). This is reflected in the modern language as prefixing stem 新 (nii-), which is no longer productive.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Attested in the Man'yōshū, completed in 759.
Derived as a compound of 新 (ara, from 生る (aru, “to come into being”), cognate also with 有り (ari, “to exist”, the Old and classical Japanese copula), 現れる (arawareru, “to appear, to become manifest”), 荒 (ara, “rough, unfinished”), numerous other terms) +‎ た (ta, suffix indicating state). The core meaning seems to have been "freshly coming into being", and by extension, new.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 新聞 (MC sin mjun). Compare Hokkien 新聞 / 新闻 (sin-bûn).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Originally clipping of 新聞紙 (shinbunshi)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: 方 (“direction”) +‎ 針 (“needle”), another name for the 磁針 (jishin, “magnetic needle”), with the meaning figuratively extending to "guidance" in general.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Reduplication of 日(ひ) (hi, “sun; day”). The hi changes to bi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
This is generally the most common reading for this kanji compound.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Reduplication of 日(にち) (nichi, “sun; day”), using the on'yomi pronunciation.
This is a less common reading for this kanji compound.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Compound of 日(ひ) (hi, “sun; day”, using the native Japanese reading) + 日(にち) (nichi, “sun; day”, using the Chinese-derived reading).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 日曜 (nichiyō, “Sun”, in reference also to the day for that celestial body, as originally imported from Chinese astrology in the Heian period) +‎ 日 (hi, “day”).
The compound form suffixed with 日 (hi, “day”) first appears in 1826 and enters common use from the Meiji period with the promulgation of the Gregorian calendar.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Appears to be a compound of Classical Japanese 明る (akaru, “to brighten”) +‎ し (shi, “adjectival suffix”). This adjectival suffix forms a classical ク活用 (ku-katsuyō, “ku-adjective”).
First attested in 1689.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Shift in meaning from 朝 (ashita, “next morning”), itself cognate with 朝 (asa, “morning”).
The kanji spelling is from Chinese 明日 (míngrì).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki (712 CE).
Various theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation:
Possibly a shift from verb 明かす (akasu, “to pass”).
*/akasu/ → */akusu/ → /asu/
Possibly an apophonic form of or cognate with 朝 (asa, “morning”).
The kanji spelling is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 明日.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/mʲau nʲiti/ → /mʲɔːɲit͡ɕi/ → /mʲoːɲit͡ɕi/
From Middle Chinese compound 明日 (MC mjaeng nyit).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
From a later borrowing of Chinese 明日 (míngrì), using the 漢音 (kan'on, literally “Han sound”).
Rare reading.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Compound of し (shi, of uncertain derivation) +‎ 明後日 (asatte, “the day after tomorrow”).
The initial shi element is uncertain. Speculatively, this might be related to, or a shift from, intensifying prefix ひ (hi) found in some adjectives, such as ひ弱(よわ)い (hiyowai, “delicate, very weak”).
First cited to a text from 1275.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Compound of 明 (myō, “next, one later”) +‎ 明後日 (myōgonichi, “day after tomorrow”).
First cited to the Nippo Jisho of 1603.

The Singapore sense derives from the pre-World War Two kanji spelling 星加坡 (modern kanji spelling 新加坡) as borrowed from Chinese, itself a transliteration of Malay Singapura.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 昨夜 (MC dzak yaeH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Shift from 夕べ (yūbe, “evening”), which has an additional 平板型 (heiban-gata) or [0] accent pitch.
The kanji spelling is from sakuya above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 土圭 (tʰuoX kwei, literally “earth, clay + stack of clay tablets”, a kind of sundial used in the Zhou Dynasty).
The 土圭 spelling is the original form, with the kan'on reading of tokei. This has been largely superseded by the spelling 時計 in modern writing, which uses the 時 character as ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)). Probably this spelling from native Japanese word ときはかり(see below). Alternatively, the kanji spelling could be interpreted as jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), using the meanings of the characters as 時 (“time”) + 計 (“measurement”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 時(とき) (toki, “time”) + 計(はか)り (hakari, “measuring”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 計(はか)る (hakaru, “to measure”).).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
時間 on Japanese Wikipedia
Probably originally borrowed from Middle Chinese compound 時間 (dzyi kɛn, literally “time interval”). Repurposed in the early Meiji period as a translation of the western term time in relation to philosophy in the 1881 publication of 哲学字彙 (Tetsugaku Jii, “Philosophy Dictionary”) compiled by Inoue Tetsujirō. The meaning "hour" can be analyzed as a compound of 時(じ) (ji, “o'clock”) + 間(かん) (-kan, time interval suffix). Compare other terms formed with the suffix 間(かん) (-kan) like 三(さん)分(ぷん)間(かん) (sanpunkan) and 三日(みっか)間(かん) (mikkakan).
The reading is a mix of the goon reading ji and the kan'on reading kan, suggesting either that the reading changed after borrowing (from the expected goon pronunciation of jiken or the expected kan'on pronunciation of shikan), or that this term was independently coined in Japanese after the constituent terms 時(じ) (ji) and 間(かん) (kan) were borrowed.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Pronunciation shift to a devoiced initial consonant in certain dialects.
/d͡ʑikaɴ/ → /t͡ɕikaɴ/

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The kanji spelling is phonetic ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)); originally written as 不断(ふだん) (fudan).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Derived from 気(け)色(しき) (keshiki).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 景色 (MC kjaengX srik).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: First attested in the late 800s. Appears to be a borrowing from Middle Chinese 書齋 (MC syo tsreaj, “a reading room, a study”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text:
⟨tuki2⟩ → */tukɨ/ → */t͡sukɨ/ → /t͡suki/
From Old Japanese 月 (tuki2), ultimately from Proto-Japonic *tukui.
For the vowel alternation, see WT:AJPX#Standalone forms and combining forms.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text:
/ɡʷatɨ/ → /ɡʷat͡su/ → /ɡat͡su/
From Middle Chinese 月 (ŋʉɐt̚).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3 2
etymologies.text:
/ɡʷetu/ → /ɡet͡su/
From Middle Chinese 月 (ŋʉɐt̚).
Compare modern Hakka 月 (ngie̍t), Min Nan 月 (ge̍h).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4 2
etymologies.text:
/ɡʷat͡ɕi/ → /ɡat͡ɕi/
First attested in the Edo period.
Appears to be a poetic use of the 呉(ご)音(おん) (goon, literally “Wu sound”) reading, in reference to a rank of 端(はし)女(じょ)郎(ろう) (hashi jorō, “low-end prostitute]”) in the Kansai region. According to a popular song, a 月(がち) (gachi, “moon”) prostitute cost one 匁(もんめ) (monme, old unit of currency, worth roughly 3.75 grams of silver), a 影(かげ) (kage, “shadow”) prostitute cost two monme, and a 汐(しお) (shio, “tide; loveliness”) prostitute cost three monme.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text: Either a shift in sense from the low-ranking prostitute meaning above, or a shift in pronunciation from 頑(がん)痴(ち) (ganchi, literally “stubborn and stupid”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Compound of 月 (tsuki, “moon, month”) +‎ 日 (hi, “sun, day”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 月 (gatsu, “month”) +‎ 日 (hi, “day”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/getueubi/ > /getuyoːbi/.
Compound of 月曜 (getsuyō, “moon”, in reference also to the day for that celestial body, as originally imported from Chinese astrology in the Heian period) +‎ 日 (hi, “day”).
The compound form suffixed with 日 (hi, “day”) appears in common use from the Meiji period with the promulgation of the Gregorian calendar. See also Names of the days of the week on Wikipedia.Wikipedia

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
⟨ki2⟩ → */kɨ/ → /ki/
From Old Japanese 木 (ki2), from Proto-Japonic *kəi. Cognate with Proto-Ryukyuan *ke. For the vowel alternation, see Wiktionary:About Proto-Japonic § Standalone forms and combining forms.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
⟨ko2⟩ → */kə/ → /ko/
From Old Japanese 木 (ko2).
Likely the original form of ki above. Obsolete in modern Japanese, never found in isolation; only found in compounds and certain idioms.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 木 (MC muwk). Compare modern Cantonese 木 (muk6).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 木 (MC muwk). Compare literary Min Nan 木 (bo̍k).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/mokueubi/ > /mokujoːbi/.
Compound of 木曜 (mokuyō, “Jupiter (the planet)”, in reference also to the day for that planet, as originally imported from Chinese astrology in the Heian period) +‎ 日 (hi, “day”).
The compound form suffixed with 日 (hi, “day”) appears in common use from the Meiji period with the promulgation of the Gregorian calendar.

Compound of 木 (ki, “tree”) +‎ 綿 (wata, “batting”).
First attested in 1589.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:木綿
Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Cotton
Wikipedia
/mokumen/ → */moɡumen/ → /moɴmen/ → /momen/
Alteration of mokumen via attested form monmen, itself derived from Middle Chinese-derived elements 木 (moku, “tree”) + 綿 (men, “cotton”).
The earlier form monmen is attested in 1468 with a sense of "cotton fibre", with the medial gemination eliding into momen by 1560.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/mokumen/ → /moɴmen/
Sound shift from expected mokumen reading, with the ku assimilating with the following nasal m. First attested in 1468.
Appears to have been superseded after the non-geminate form momen arose in 1560. May be obsolete in modern usage; this reading is not included in many dictionaries.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:木綿 (ゆう)
Wikipedia ja
/jupu/ → /jufu/ → */juwu/ → /juː/
From Old Japanese.
Possibly from the verb 結う (yuu, “to tie up”), from the way such strings are used to tie sakaki branches in Shinto rituals. (Can this(+) etymology be sourced?) Compare the development of 夕 (yū, “evening”).
The kanji spelling is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), likely from the similar texture and consistency of cotton.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:未来
Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Future
Wikipedia
From Middle Chinese 未來 (MC mj+jH loj). Originally a Buddhist calque of Sanskrit अनागत (anāgata, “not yet come; future”, past participle), from अन्- (an-, “not”) + आगत (āgata, “what has come”), from the verb root आगम् (āgam, “to come”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Compound of 未 (mi, the on'yomi or Chinese-derived reading) +‎ 来 (ku, the kun'yomi or native Japanese reading).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Compound of 未 (mi, the on'yomi or Chinese-derived reading) +‎ 来る (kuru, the kun'yomi or native Japanese reading).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Shift from earlier 末(すえ)子(こ) (sueko), from 末 (sue, “end”) +‎ 子 (ko, “child”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mura.
Either formed from the nominalization of 群れる (mureru, “to gather”), or from Old Korean. In Old Korean toponyms, this appears with the phonetic spelling 牟羅 (*mura). Compare Korean 무리 (muri, “group, crowd”), also possibly cognate with 群れる (mureru, “to gather”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 村 (MC tshwon).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 東西 (MC tuwng sej). (Can this(+) etymology be sourced?)
The sai reading for 西 changes to zai as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First mentioned in the Man'yōshū, completed in 759 CE.
Derives from the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 生やす (hayasu, “to grow”). The root verb is in the transitive form, suggesting that the original sense of hayashi may have indicated a deliberately planted or managed grove.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/rimʉ/ → /riɴ/
From Middle Chinese 林 (MC lim).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
果物 on Japanese Wikipedia
果物 (kudamono, kabutsu): various kinds of fruit.
Literally “tree's thing”. Originally a compound of 木 (ku, “tree”, irregular shift from ancient ko pronunciation) +‎ だ (da, possessive marker between two nouns, only found in a few compounds) +‎ 物 (mono, “thing”).
The medial da is also seen in 獣 (kedamono, “beast”, literally “hairy thing”). The kanji is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/kwabut͡su/ → /kabut͡su/
Possibly from Middle Chinese compound 果物 (*kuɑ *miuət, literally “fruit thing”). Compare modern Mandarin 果物 reading guǒwù (rare), Cantonese gwo2 mat6 (rare).
Rarely used in modern Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Coined or borrowed from Chinese 營養 (yíngyǎng, “to nourish the body”) in the end of the Edo period. Both spellings 栄養 and 営養 were used until the establishment of 栄養研究所 (“the Institute of Nutrition”) in the Home Ministry in 1920 and the publication of 『栄養』 by Japanese scientist Tadasu Saiki in 1926, and thence 栄養 has been mainly used.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
桜 (sakura): the Japanese cherry tree, Prunus serrulata

Wikipedia ja
English Wikipedia has an article on:Prunus serrulata
